messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Three years ago, during a break between rehearsals, Naomi was waiting on a subway platform when she witnessed a police officer shoot a man during a struggle. The sound was deafening; she saw the man fall and the officer stand over him. She could not move, could not scream—she was a bystander, frozen, while others fled. In the days after, her memories came only in fragments: the officer’s raised gun, the man’s face slack, the smell of metal. She could not put the event into words; when she tried to tell a friend, the story would not form. The officer was cleared, and no one was held accountable, and Naomi came to believe that the people responsible had faced no consequences at all. That injustice lodged itself in her chest, and she began to feel permanently set apart from others—an outsider who could never rejoin the safety of ordinary life.

Because she was certain that violence could go unpunished, Naomi found it impossible to trust that she was safe, even when others told her she was fine. The world felt openly hostile. Her conviction that the shooter faced no consequences kept the memory alive: the fragments played more often, more vividly, as if the injustice itself forced the scene to replay. Each time a piece of the memory surfaced—the flash of the gun, the crowd’s screams—her heart would race, and she would be flooded with fear, then anger, then the familiar shame of having done nothing. Her persistent fear convinced her she was permanently vulnerable, which deepened her belief that she was isolated and beyond protection.

Naomi began to choose where she sat based on how safe she felt—always with her back to a wall, always near an exit. At auditions and rehearsals, she scanned the room for anything that reminded her of that day. Military and police uniforms, even weapons used as props, triggered a visceral panic. She stopped taking the subway entirely, convinced the next violence was waiting. When casting calls involved police gear or location shoots near public transit, she declined—each refusal costing her work but reinforcing that she was no longer part of the normal world. To distract herself from the crushing isolation, she started spending impulsively: new clothes, expensive dinners, anything to fill the hours when the memories threatened. But the spending only made her feel more disconnected from her savings and from people who did not understand why a stable actress would sabotage her career.

The more she avoided the subway and uniforms, the more threatening they became—she never learned that public transport could be safe. Her avoidance also left her feeling even more cut off from colleagues who still took the train to the theater, and their casual conversations about commutes became reminders of her difference. The isolation deepened her sense of being an outsider, which in turn made the fragmented memories feel more vivid and inescapable. The fear kept the event alive, and the memory kept the fear fresh—a loop that tightened every week.

Last month, Naomi turned down a role in a film that required a scene at a train station. Her agent told her she was limiting herself, and the director asked why she kept passing up good work. She had no words. That night, she found herself online, searching for therapists who specialized in trauma. What frightened her most was the thought that she might never get back on the subway—that the outsider she had become was permanent. She wanted to act again, to go to a rehearsal without scanning for exits. But she also feared that if she tried to talk about the shooting, the fragments would turn into something even worse, something she could not control.
